title.value: Robust Threshold ECDSA with Online-Friendly Design in Three Rounds
Robust Threshold ECDSA with Online-Friendly Design in Three Rounds

abstract.value: Threshold signatures, especially ECDSA, enhance key protection by addressing the single-point-of-failure issue. Threshold signing can be divided into offline and online phases, based on whether the message is required. Schemes with lowcost online phases are referred to as "online-friendly". Another critical aspect of threshold ECDSA for real-world applications is robustness, which guarantees the successful completion of each signing execution whenever a threshold number t of semihonest participants is met, even in the presence of misbehaving signatories. The state-of-the-art online-friendly threshold ECDSA without robustness was developed by Doerner et al. in S&P'24, requiring only three rounds. Recent work by Wong et al. in NDSS'23 (WMY + 23) and NDSS'24 (WMC24) achieves robustness but demands additional communication rounds (7 and 4, respectively) or incurs costly operations in the online phase, such as computations over a homomorphic encryption scheme. This paper presents the first three-round threshold ECDSA scheme with both robustness and an online-friendly design. The online phase of our scheme relies solely on several ellipticcurve group operations, which are 2 to 3 orders of magnitude less computationally intensive than those based on linearly homomorphic encryption schemes. We implement our protocol and conduct a comprehensive comparison with WMY + 23 and WMC24. Benchmark results show that the online phase of our scheme is 2.5× faster than that of WMY + 23 and hundreds of times faster than that of WMC24. Lastly, we demonstrate that our techniques can be extended to construct an online-friendly and robust three-round threshold BBS+ scheme. 203 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

Threshold signatures, especially ECDSA, enhance key protection by addressing the single-point-of-failure issue. Threshold signing can be divided into offline and online phases, based on whether the message is required. Schemes with low- cost online phases are referred to as “online-friendly”. Another critical aspect of threshold ECDSA for real-world applications is robustness, which guarantees the successful completion of each signing execution whenever a threshold number t of semi- honest participants is met, even in the presence of misbehaving signatories. The state-of-the-art online-friendly threshold ECDSA with- out robustness was developed by Doerner et al. in S&P'24, requiring only three rounds. Recent work by Wong et al. in NDSS'23 (WMY +23) and NDSS'24 (WMC24) achieves robustness but demands additional communication rounds (7 and 4, respectively) or incurs costly operations in the online phase, such as computations over a homomorphic encryption scheme. This paper presents the first three-round threshold ECDSA scheme with both robustness and an online-friendly design. The online phase of our scheme relies solely on several elliptic- curve group operations, which are 2 to 3 orders of magnitude less computationally intensive than those based on linearly homomorphic encryption schemes. We implement our protocol and conduct a comprehensive comparison with WMY +23 and WMC24. Benchmark results show that the online phase of our scheme is 2.5× faster than that of WMY +23 and hundreds of times faster than that of WMC24. Lastly, we demonstrate that our techniques can be extended to construct an online-friendly and robust three-round threshold BBS+ scheme. 1. Introduction A (t, n) threshold signature [33] splits the signing key across n parties, such that: (1) any subset of t honest parties can produce a valid signature without reconstructing the key, and (2) any subset of fewer than t parties can not [43], [53]. Threshold signatures provide enhanced key protection by mitigating the risk of single points of failure, making them highly valuable in both blockchain applications and academic research. Their significance can be recognized from NIST's upcoming standardization efforts on Multi- Party Threshold Cryptography [16]. With the rising demand for blockchain-based cryptocur- rencies, the design and deployment of threshold ECDSA have seen widespread popularity over the past decade. This includes seminal contributions by [34], [36], [41], [47], [48] and implementations by industry like Coinbase [3], Binance [1], Zengo [5], BitGo [2], and Fireblocks [4]. Cheater Identification & Robustness. The fundamental security requirement for threshold ECDSA is the ability to tolerate up to t − 1 malicious (or corrupted) participants. Beyond this basic security, additional features are valuable in practice, such as cheater identification [8], [20], [25], [40] and robustness [57], [58]. Cheater identification (also known as identifiable abort if abort after identification) allows for the detection of misbehaving parties. Typically, we can design a protocol that eliminates the cheaters and restarts the signing process until a signature is produced. This will cause the round count to be related to the number of corruptions, which is unacceptable especially in time-sensitive applications. Even worse, the signature string can be biasable by the adversary, which is an attack if it is used for leader election. Therefore, they propose the robustness feature, which, after identifying cheaters, allows the signing process to continue and produce a valid signature as long as the re- maining (semi)honest parties still meet the threshold t. It is worth noting, as analyzed in [30], that an honest majority (n ≥ 2t−1) appears to be necessary for achieving robustness (i.e., the public key and/or signatures are not adversarially biased). Online and Offline Signing. In general, it is highly ad- vantageous to separate a multiparty computation (MPC) protocol into offline and online phases. During the offline phase, input-independent computations are performed and can be batched during idle CPU time. The results from the offline phase are stored for future use in the online phase, when specific inputs become available, with the goal of minimizing the online computational cost. An example is the use of Beaver triples [9] to facilitate efficient computation of multiplication gates in the online phase. The same principle applies to threshold ECDSA protocols, which can be divided into offline (pre-signing) and online phases, depending on whether the signing message is required. The goal is to make online signing efficient by shifting computationally intensive tasks to the offline phase, such as Multiplicative-to-Additive 203 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00115 (MtA) conversions. Protocols are considered online-friendly if the online phase requires only minimal elliptic curve (EC) group operations, as in [25], [36], [58]. Others [23], [47], [57] rely on costly operations with linearly homomor- phic encryption (LHE) in the online phase. Notably, some schemes [20] are online-friendly but still require expensive operations for cheater identification. Current Threshold ECDSAs. To motivate our work, we briefly introduce existing threshold ECDSA schemes based on different building blocks and discuss their pros and cons regarding rounds, online complexity, cheater identification, and robustness. OT-based schemes. Doerner et al. proposed a series of threshold ECDSA schemes based on Oblivious Transfer (OT) [34], [35], [36]. These schemes have very fast running times but require substantial bandwidth (over 49.7n KB when n parties are involved). The most advanced among them, [36] (hereafter referred to as DKLs24), achieves three communication rounds and extremely low online costs. However, it can only achieve basic security without identi- fiable abort or robustness. Recently, Cohen et al. [31] added identifiable abort to DKLs24, but it requires seven rounds of communication. LHE-based scheme. Linearly homomorphic encryption (LHE) is another common building block of threshold ECDSA, such as Paillier encryption (e.g., [11], [41], [42], [47], [48]), Castagnos-Laguillaumie encryption (CL, e.g., [24], [25]), and Joye-Libert encryption (JL, e.g., [59]). These constructions have low bandwidth but require higher computation overhead compared to those from OT. Some LHE-based solutions enable cheater identification, as in CGG+20 [20], and robustness, as in WMY +23 [58]. How- ever, CGG+20 suffers from expensive online cheater iden- tification, and WMY +23 requires seven rounds to achieve robustness. TLHE-based scheme. Inspired by [17], WMC24 [57] pro- poses a threshold ECDSA scheme with cheater identification and robustness by employing threshold CL encryption. It achieves a constant (sending) communication overhead for each participant. However, due to the threshold decryp- tion operations and the associated zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs), the scheme is not online-friendly and requires at least four communication rounds. We provide a comparison of state-of-the-art works in each category in Table 1, evaluating them based on rounds, cheater identification (CI), robustness, and online cost. In summary, current constructions either achieve a three-round, online-friendly design but lack CI and robustness, or they provide CI and/or robustness at the expense of additional rounds and/or higher online costs. This paper is therefore motivated by the goal of designing a three-round threshold ECDSA scheme that incorporates CI, robustness, and low online cost. TABLE 1: Comparisons of threshold ECDSAs, in terms of rounds, CI (cheater identification), R (robustness) and online cost. “Optimal” indicates the online phase (OP) has no more EC group operations except for signature verifica- tion. “Enc”, “Dec”, “Paillier-ZKP”, and “CL-ZKP” indicate encryption, decryption, Paillier or CL-related ZKPs. “DDH- ZKP” means ZKPs for DDH relation. The OPs of [25], [31], [58] require ZKPs over the EC group for relations more complex than DDH, which can be considered approximately as 2× or 3× DDH-ZKP. 1.1. Our Contributions We present an online-friendly robust threshold ECDSA which requires three rounds, comparable with the state- of-the-art scheme without robustness. We also extend our technique to thresholding BBS+ [7], a crucial primitive for anonymous credential issuance. • As shown in Table 1, current techniques for adding ro- bustness to threshold ECDSA [57], [58] require at least one extra round to the already three-round signing phase. We successfully achieve CI and robustness without addi- tional rounds. Moreover, the online phase of our protocol relies on only a few elliptic curve operations. Two novel techniques are developed to achieve this. a) Our main observation is that an undetermined tem- porary secret nonce 1 is sufficient for robust threshold ECDSA. Using this indeterminacy allows us to avoid the additional round of interaction needed to generate a determined temporary secret nonce 2, as required in [58]. Despite the undetermined nature, the signato- ries can still successfully assemble the signature (i.e., achieve robustness) because the value will ultimately be canceled out. b) Furthermore, in the online phase, we use a simple zero-knowledge proof for the decisional Diffie-Hellman (DDH) relation , which requires only inexpensive el- liptic curve operations. This zero-knowledge proof is more cost-effective than those required in the online phases of [57]. Notably, the DDH-relation proof en- 1. An undetermined secret nonce is shared into additive shares (e.g., r = Pn i=1 ri). The value assembled by one set of parties differs from that assembled by another. As malicious parties are removed, the set of signers is undetermined. Thus, the value is also undetermined. 2. A determined secret nonce is shared in the t-threshold form using Shamir's secret sharing. The value assembled by any ≥ t parties is determined. 204
